text: Taliban releases biography of reclusive leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, asserting he remains alive and in command. The 11-page document aims to counter persistent death rumors and reassert Omar's jihadi credentials amid a leadership challenge from ISIS's self-declared caliph. It details his early life, battlefield exploits, and current daily schedule, but omits past ties to al Qaeda.

Hundreds of mourners gathered in Summerville for the funeral of Walter Scott, whose videotaped shooting by a North Charleston officer sparked calls for change. Clergy and family framed Scott’s death as a catalyst against racial prejudice in policing. Former officer Michael Slager has been charged with murder and faces life in prison or the death penalty.

A former TSA agent was sentenced to six months in jail for secretly recording a female co-worker in a bathroom and illegally entering her home. Daniel Boykin pleaded guilty after police found over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim on his devices. The judge called the invasion of privacy "egregious" and also imposed five and a half years of probation with GPS monitoring.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to boost its economy, lacking conventional natural resources. Events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and the Atlantic Music Expo aim to give local artists international exposure and attract tourism. Officials and industry figures believe promoting the country's culture is a cost-effective way to drive future economic growth.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 to close within four points of leader Chelsea ahead of their title clash. Aston Villa and Leicester earned vital wins in the relegation fight, while Crystal Palace thrashed Sunderland 4-1.

Twin Peaks cast members released a video backing David Lynch’s salary standoff with Showtime, warning a revival without him is “like pies without cherries.” Lynch exited the nine-episode revival citing insufficient funds, while Showtime said it still hopes to bring the project back with both creators.

Andrew Getty, 47-year-old heir to the Getty oil fortune, was found dead in his home, with police saying preliminary findings point to natural causes and no foul play. Authorities noted he had several health issues and medication was recovered from the residence, while an autopsy is pending.

Nyia Parler, 41, cannot be extradited to Philadelphia to face charges for allegedly abandoning her quadriplegic son in the woods until she completes unspecified treatment in Maryland. Her 21-year-old son, who has cerebral palsy, was found after four days suffering from dehydration and malnutrition. Parler faces charges including aggravated assault once she is transferred.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai to honor the education activist. The asteroid, designated 316201 Malala, is about 4 kilometers in diameter and orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter. Mainzer noted few asteroids have been named to honor contributions of women, particularly women of color.

A gastrointestinal outbreak has sickened 100 people aboard the Celebrity Infinity cruise ship. The CDC reports 95 passengers and 5 crew are affected, though the cause remains undetermined. The vessel is scheduled to be met by CDC staff in San Diego on Monday.

"Star Wars" saga released on digital HD. Mindy Kaling's brother reveals he faked being black for medical school admission, drawing family disapproval. A couple named Burger and King scored a free Burger King wedding.

FBI charged a Philadelphia woman for attempting to travel overseas to join ISIS, one of three women arrested this week on terror charges. She allegedly expressed a desire for martyrdom online and purchased a ticket to Barcelona as a cover before her arrest. The arrests highlight a growing trend of domestic lone-wolf cases involving social media and support for ISIS.

HBO released a teaser for "True Detective" season two, premiering June 21. The new season stars Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch in a California-set conspiracy involving a bizarre murder. The first season was a critical and ratings hit for the network.

Carlos Colina, 32, was charged Monday after human remains belonging to Jonathan Camilien, 26, were found in a duffel bag and an apartment building common area in Cambridge. Authorities identified the victim and said the two men knew each other. Colina faces assault and improper disposal charges pending further investigation.

Louisville high school basketball star Trey Moses asked freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to prom in a viral "prom-posal." Moses, praised for his character, plans to study special education at Ball State. Ellie's mother said the gesture brought relief after years of social struggles for her daughter.

NBC premieres "A.D. The Bible Continues," a 12-week miniseries sequel to History's hit "The Bible," this Sunday. The week also marks the final season premiere of "Mad Men" and the debut of Netflix's Marvel drama "Daredevil."

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence’s signing of a religious freedom law, despite backlash, is seen as a move to shore up conservative credentials for a 2016 presidential run. The controversy is forcing the entire Republican field to adopt harder-line stances against LGBT rights, ensuring the issue will feature prominently in the primary. Analysts warn the debate could alienate general election voters despite recent national shifts toward same-sex marriage.

Apple released a new mobile OS update adding emojis with diverse skin tones, same-sex couples, and additional flags. The move drew both praise and criticism, including past objections over a non-white Santa and complaints from groups still unrepresented. The update is seen as a step toward reflecting America’s changing demographics in digital communication.

Avril Lavigne revealed she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease from a tick bite last spring. The singer said she struggled to breathe, talk, and move before doctors diagnosed her, and she is now “80 percent better.” Lavigne is releasing a new single this month and says the illness gave her a new perspective on life.

New research from the Anne Frank House indicates Anne and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than previously believed, likely in February 1945 rather than March. Researchers re-examined archives and survivor testimonies, concluding the sisters probably succumbed to typhus before February 7 based on witness accounts of their symptoms. The exact dates of death remain unclear.

Two Troy University students were arrested for allegedly gang raping a woman during spring break in Panama City Beach. The assault was discovered after Alabama police found a video during an unrelated shooting investigation. Both men have been suspended from the university pending further legal proceedings.

A Washington state stray dog survived being hit by a car, struck with a hammer, and buried for four days before staggering to a nearby farm. The one-year-old bully breed mix, now named Theia, is receiving veterinary care for severe injuries including a dislocated jaw and caved-in sinus cavity. A fundraiser for her treatment has surpassed its goal, with excess funds to be donated to help other animals.

FBI confirms DNA tests prove Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in January's Philippine raid. The operation, which killed the wanted terrorist, went disastrously wrong, resulting in the deaths of 44 elite police commandos. The botched mission has jeopardized a fragile peace agreement with the main Muslim rebel group.

A U.S. lawmaker warns the Iran nuclear framework gives Tehran sanctions relief while preserving its nuclear infrastructure and lacks tough inspection safeguards. The author argues Congress' tougher sanctions strategy was blocked, and fears the deal repeats failed North Korea-style verification.

"Mad Men" begins its final episodes Sunday, concluding AMC's acclaimed drama about a 1960s ad agency navigating social upheaval. The season is expected to pick up after the July 1969 moon landing, with characters facing professional uncertainty and personal reckonings. Creator Matthew Weiner has kept plot details secret, leaving fans to speculate on the fates of Don Draper and his colleagues.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth to a roughly 6-foot-tall calf Friday evening during a live-streamed labor watched online via Animal Planet. The newborn showed positive signs such as moving its ears and attempting to nurse, though its gender and condition were not immediately released. The birth followed a 15-month gestation and was witnessed by other giraffes, including Katie’s companion Jade.

Loretta Lynch's confirmation as attorney general has stalled in the Senate for six months, longer than the past eight nominees combined. Supporters and some lawmakers allege race is a factor in the delay, while Republicans blame partisan disputes over immigration and a trafficking bill.

Armed assailants stormed the attorney general’s office in Afghanistan’s Balkh province, killing three and wounding five. Most staff and civilians have been rescued, but an ongoing firefight continues as security forces advance cautiously.
Bob Barker returned to host a segment of “The Price Is Right” for the first time since retiring in 2007. The 91-year-old emceed the opening game before handing duties back to current host Drew Carey.

Blues legend B.B. King was briefly hospitalized for dehydration related to his Type II diabetes but has since been released and is resting at home. The 89-year-old guitarist thanked fans for their concern and said he is feeling much better.

Jurors convicted Dzhokhar Tsarnaev on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. The article argues that preventing future attacks requires understanding radicalization as a political exploitation of Muslim grievances, not an inherent flaw in Islam. It contends extremism will be defeated by showing young Muslims that violence harms rather than helps their community.

A CNN weekly video roundup features a tour of Mike Tyson's former Ohio mansion, now set to become a church. Other highlights include a ride on the world's tallest giga-coaster and a CNN exclusive interview with Bikram yoga students alleging sexual assault. The collection also covers a witness account of the Germanwings crash and a debate on Indiana's religious freedom law.

The Pentagon released a map showing coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory previously held by ISIS, with gains concentrated in central and northern Iraq. A counterinsurgency expert cautioned that territorial gains against ISIS are strategically significant but that the group is adapting by staging high-profile attacks elsewhere to distract from losses. He also noted the coalition’s current strategy relies on frontal pushes rather than more creative maneuver warfare to break up ISIS-held areas.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight to Atlanta attempted to choke a sleeping man with a cord, claiming the victim was trying to kill him. Fellow passengers intervened to stop the attack, and the suspect was escorted off the plane by authorities for a mental evaluation. No federal charges are currently pending.

A British former banker is charged with murdering two Indonesian women in his Hong Kong apartment. The court adjourned until May to allow forensic analysis of over 200 pieces of evidence. One victim was found with neck wounds, the other inside a suitcase on the balcony.
Multiple tornadoes struck the rural Midwest, killing one person in Fairdale, Illinois, and destroying dozens of homes. Officials reported widespread damage but said early warnings likely saved lives.

Don McLean's original handwritten lyrics to "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's, the third-highest price ever for an American literary manuscript. The 16-page draft includes unused lines and notes. McLean said he sold it to provide for his family.

UNRWA’s chief makes an emergency visit to Syria’s Yarmouk camp on Saturday to assess the dire humanitarian situation for 18,000 trapped civilians. The camp, largely controlled by ISIS and Al-Nusra Front, has been cut off from aid since 2013 amid widespread malnutrition and ongoing conflict.

Saudi-led airstrikes in Sanaa have destroyed infrastructure and cut power to 16 million, while ground fighting killed over 50 in Aden on Monday alone. The ICRC is demanding a humanitarian ceasefire as medical supplies remain grounded, with an estimated 600 dead since the campaign began. Deposed President Hadi, now in Saudi Arabia, fired his former army chief who had already defected to the Houthi rebels.

Richie Benaud, former Australia cricket captain and iconic broadcaster, has died aged 84 after battling skin cancer. He was revered worldwide for his record-breaking playing career and peerless commentary, with tributes from leaders and cricketers. Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott said flags would fly at half-mast on the day of his funeral.

A total lunar eclipse, the shortest of the century at 4 minutes and 43 seconds, began over western North America early Saturday. The "blood moon" is the third in a tetrad of eclipses, with the best views west of the Mississippi River.

Robert Durst, the real estate heir and subject of HBO's "The Jinx," has been indicted on a federal weapons charge for possessing a revolver found in his New Orleans hotel room. The 71-year-old, who faces a separate first-degree murder charge in Los Angeles for the 2000 killing of Susan Berman, could receive up to 10 years in prison if convicted on the gun charge.

Paul Walker died in a 2013 car crash during a break from filming "Furious 7." The film, which releases Friday, completes his character's story using rewrites, special effects and his brothers as stand-ins, in what his co-star Vin Diesel calls an emotional tribute. Fans and colleagues remember Walker for his humility and off-screen generosity.

A model on "The Price Is Right" accidentally revealed a car's price, giving it to the contestant. Host Drew Carey laughed it off, and the model later said all was well. The gaffe came a day after former host Bob Barker's return.

Thai Smile unveiled an Airbus A320 adorned with "Adventure Time" characters in a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone water park. The themed aircraft features Jake, Finn, and Princess Bubblegum on its exterior and cabin interior. The inaugural flight departs Bangkok for Phuket on April 4.

CNN crew and bystanders rescued a brood of ducklings and their mother from a busy Washington street. Pedestrians used an umbrella to corral the birds and stopped traffic so they could safely cross. The family was relocated to a nearby enclosed grassy area.

French investigators have finished collecting main evidence from the Germanwings crash site and do not plan to return. A private security firm will guard the area until remaining debris is removed. The flight data recorder shows co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately accelerated the plane’s descent, and he had hidden medical notes declaring him unfit to work.

Cuba and the U.S. attend the Summit of the Americas together for the first time since 1962 amid a historic diplomatic thaw. The summit offers a chance to advance embassy re-openings, though Cuba demands removal from the U.S. terrorism list. A street brawl between Cuban government supporters and dissidents in Panama marred Cuba's rebranding efforts.

Jesus and his disciples likely lived at subsistence level, relying on begging, hospitality, and donations. Key financial backers included wealthy women like Joanna and Mary Magdalene, who used their own resources to support the ministry. Affluent men such as Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus may also have contributed.

California regulators ordered PG&E to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas pipeline operations linked to the deadly 2010 San Bruno explosion. The penalty primarily forces the utility to spend $850 million on pipeline safety upgrades. The blast killed eight people and destroyed 37 homes.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old college basketball player who inspired millions by playing despite terminal brain cancer, has died. She realized her dream of playing for Mount St. Joseph University and helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research. Her coach called her "an unselfish angel" who taught others how to live.

A massive fire erupted Friday morning at GE Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, with no reported injuries. The four-alarm blaze sent thick smoke and flames skyward as firefighters worked to contain it. The cause remains unknown.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, hailed for his role in nuclear talks, has a complex background including US education, disputed birth year, and past federal investigation. He previously engaged in revolutionary-era consulate takeovers and has spent more time with John Kerry than any other foreign minister.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to release a 17-year-old girl from state custody, keeping her in a hospital to complete court-ordered chemotherapy. The teen, now in remission for Hodgkin lymphoma, will remain confined until her final treatment round concludes this month. Her attorneys are considering an appeal.

Computer-aided textual analysis suggests "Double Falsehood," a play long dismissed as a forgery, was largely written by William Shakespeare with contributions from John Fletcher. Researchers identified a clear psychological signature matching Shakespeare in the first half of the play, and a mix of Shakespeare and Fletcher in the latter portion. The study's objective, data-driven approach offers new evidence in the centuries-old authorship debate.

French prosecutor Brice Robin said no video from inside Germanwings Flight 9525 has been used in the crash investigation, despite reports by Bild and Paris Match claiming such footage exists. French officials called the reports “completely wrong,” while the publications stood by their accounts. Lufthansa also confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had disclosed a prior episode of severe depression during pilot training.

American Samoans, born on U.S. soil, are denied citizenship under a policy rooted in racist "Insular Cases" precedent. A decorated veteran is leading a federal lawsuit to overturn this exception to the 14th Amendment's birthright citizenship guarantee. A D.C. Circuit ruling is imminent in the fight to end this last remaining vestige of second-class territorial status.

Blue Bell has halted production at its Oklahoma plant after listeria was found in ice cream cups from the facility. The CDC warns against consuming 3-ounce institutional servings from the plant, though the contamination has not been definitively linked to a Kansas outbreak that killed three. This marks the third recent recall action for the company.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for a deadly attack on Kenya's Garissa University College, marking a further escalation in regional instability. The Somalia-based group exploits local grievances and exclusion alongside its radical Islamist ideology. Lasting security requires addressing deeper political and economic problems fueling the insurgency.

The U.S. is lodging a diplomatic protest after a Russian Su-27 aggressively intercepted an RC-135U reconnaissance plane in international airspace over the Baltic Sea. The Pentagon deemed the high-speed, close-proximity maneuvers unsafe and unprofessional, while Moscow claimed the U.S. aircraft was flying toward its border with its transponder off.

A hooded black angel artwork appeared near the site of Walter Scott’s fatal police shooting in North Charleston, becoming a symbol for Black Lives Matter protests. Creator Phillip Hyman made the piece from reclaimed wood as an act of mourning for Scott’s family. The artwork has since been used in demonstrations outside City Hall.

Video contradicts initial police reports that Walter Scott took an officer's Taser before he was shot. Witness Feidin Santana says Scott never grabbed the Taser, and the officer appeared in control before firing eight times at the fleeing, unarmed man. Officer Michael Slager has been fired and charged with murder.

ISIS claimed Sunday to have seized part of Iraq’s largest oil refinery in Baiji, posting images of the assault, while Iraqi officials denied the claim and said forces remain in full control. The refinery, a key domestic fuel source, has been repeatedly contested and sits just 40 kilometers from Tikrit, recently retaken from ISIS.

Nashville's district attorney banned sterilization offers in plea deals after public outrage, though the practice has occurred nationwide for years. The controversy highlights a gender bias, as male sterilization via castration for sex offenders has long occurred without similar outcry. Legal experts note such deals may be constitutional because defendants can waive Eighth Amendment rights.

The Ebola epidemic has infected over 25,000 and killed more than 10,000, exposing global vulnerability and systemic flaws. While cases have plummeted to their lowest weekly total since May 2014, with Liberia decommissioning surplus treatment centers, Guinea still reports unsafe burials and unidentified post-mortem cases that could spark new chains of transmission.

The NCAA argues in court it has no legal duty to ensure the academic quality of courses for athletes, directly contradicting its long-stated principle that athletes are students first. Critics call the stance hypocritical double talk, while the NCAA likens its role to a professional association without day-to-day operational control over member schools.

An explosion at a paraxylene chemical plant in China's Fujian province injured six people and sparked a large fire now under control. The blast occurred at an oil storage facility following a leak, with no toxic spill reported. The plant was previously relocated due to public protests over pollution concerns.

A bystander's video shows a South Carolina officer shooting a fleeing, unarmed black man in the back, then appearing to plant evidence. The author argues the killing would likely have been prevented had the officer worn a body camera, which studies show reduces use-of-force incidents. While not a cure for systemic racial bias, body cameras are presented as an urgent, interim safeguard to restore public trust and break a cycle of deadly police encounters.

The Summit of the Americas in Panama, intended to showcase a U.S.-Cuba thaw, has become a "triangle of tension" as Venezuela's President Maduro rallies regional allies against U.S. sanctions. Cuba's foreign minister publicly backed Venezuela, complicating the anticipated handshake between Presidents Obama and Castro.

A nuclear submarine undergoing repairs at a Russian shipyard caught fire, with its rubber insulation burning. Officials said the reactor had been unloaded and no ammunition or dangerous materials were aboard, posing no threat. No injuries were reported.

Tropical storm Maysak, formerly a super typhoon, is approaching the Philippines with 70 mph winds, prompting evacuations and bans on outdoor activities. It is expected to make landfall Sunday on Isabela province’s southeastern coast and exit the country by Monday. Authorities warn residents to prepare for possible flash floods and landslides.

Deion Sanders publicly rebuked his son Deion Sanders Jr. on Twitter for claiming he only eats "hood doughnuts." The elder Sanders reminded his son of his privileged upbringing, citing his million-dollar trust fund, condo, and clothing line.

Guatemala faces epidemic levels of gender-based violence, ranking third globally in killings of women, fueled by a legacy of civil war impunity, deeply rooted machismo, and a weak justice system where 98% of cases never reach court. Survivors like Adelma Cifuentes are finding justice and empowerment through theater and community programs, while the government has introduced specialized femicide courts. Despite these steps, international NGOs and advocates stress that urgent action is still needed to protect millions of women trapped in cycles of abuse.

Police in Malegaon, Maharashtra, are requiring cattle owners to register their animals with photos and identifying details to help enforce a new state-wide beef ban. The measure follows a recent cow slaughter case, with penalties for killing bulls or selling beef now reaching up to five years in prison. Beef traders have protested the law with a month-long strike and plan to challenge it in court.

Lucknow police in India will deploy camera-equipped drones capable of spraying pepper spray to control violent protests and mobs. The drones, costing up to $19,300 each, have been tested successfully, though critics argue the tactic is authoritarian and avoids dialogue.

The original handwritten lyrics to Don McLean's 1971 epic "American Pie" sold at Christie's for $1.2 million. The 16-page manuscript of the eight-and-a-half-minute allegorical song about rock 'n' roll and American culture was bought by an unnamed buyer. McLean wrote the song, in part, as a response to the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson.

A daring Easter weekend heist in London's jewelry district saw thieves use old-school methods to crack a vault, echoing infamous crimes from decades past. Experts say such sophisticated raids rely on meticulous planning, inside information, and teams of trusted specialists motivated purely by financial gain. Police will now conduct a relentless forensic and intelligence investigation to track the gang.

7-Eleven is launching its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday, charging $1.49 to fill any sanitary vessel that fits through a 10-inch display hole. The promotion, distinct from the annual Free Slurpee Day, encourages customers to use creative containers from trophies to sand buckets.

Kentucky state senator Georgia Davis Powers criticizes Rand Paul's presidential bid, arguing his outreach to minorities is undermined by his opposition to voting rights, civil rights laws, and other progressive protections. She contends his record shows outdated, disqualifying views that would reverse decades of progress.

A passenger died when a Lamborghini crashed during a fantasy driving experience at Walt Disney World Speedway. The driver lost control and hit a guardrail, suffering minor injuries. The attraction's operator expressed condolences.

The defense in the Aaron Hernandez murder trial rested after calling just a single day of witnesses. Key points for the jury include testimony that Hernandez knew the time of death before it was public, his fiancee's disposal of a box from their home, and disputed analysis of footwear impressions. Closing arguments are set for Tuesday.

Chinese authorities have formally detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for "creating disturbances" after they planned an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment. The detentions come amid an ongoing crackdown on independent activism, even as Beijing prepares to adopt its first anti-domestic violence law. The activists face a legal deadline of April 13 for release or formal arrest.

Martin O'Malley dismissed Hillary Clinton's perceived inevitability, citing history's upsets. The potential presidential contender argued the Democratic field should not be limited to one candidate. He spoke while visiting Iowa, where polls show him with minimal support.

Former NFL star Aaron Hernandez was sentenced to life in prison for the first-degree murder of Odin Lloyd. Lloyd's family described him as a hardworking, devoted family man and gifted athlete. His mother expressed forgiveness for her son's killers.

Ted Cruz is aggressively courting Iowa's evangelical voters, seen as key to victory in the state's early caucuses, with a campaign style mirroring pastoral outreach. He aims to unite evangelicals with tea party and libertarian factions, betting a surge in Christian conservative turnout can propel him through a crowded GOP field.

Marvel unveiled the first full look at Paul Bettany as the android Vision in a new "Avengers: Age of Ultron" poster. The reveal capped a 24-hour superhero news blitz that also included the first real look at Netflix's Daredevil suit, the casting of Angel for "X-Men: Apocalypse," and a new image of The Thing from "Fantastic Four."

Italian coast guard rescued 978 migrants off Libya on Friday, as Mediterranean crossings surge. Over 10,000 arrivals were registered in Italy in early 2015, with at least 480 deaths so far this year. Most migrants come from West Africa, Somalia, and Syria, using Libya as a transit point.

TV5Monde regained control of one channel after a powerful cyberattack disrupted its 11 channels, websites, and social media accounts. The network said it was hacked by an Islamist group, with ISIS logos appearing on its accounts, though no group claimed responsibility.

David Lynch has withdrawn from directing the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient funding from Showtime to produce the series properly. Showtime expressed sadness but remains hopeful Lynch can be brought back to helm the project alongside co-creator Mark Frost.

High-profile trials for Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev near their conclusions in Massachusetts. Senator Rand Paul officially launched his 2016 presidential bid, while Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel faces a tough runoff election. Ferguson, Missouri, holds city council elections under the shadow of the Michael Brown case.

Tornadoes touched down in Kansas and Missouri overnight, with spotters reporting twisters near Wichita and damage in Potosi. Forecasters warn of more severe storms across the Midwest and Mississippi River Valley on Thursday.

Jodi Arias sentenced to life without parole for the 2008 murder of Travis Alexander. The judge imposed the sentence after two separate juries deadlocked on the death penalty. Arias expressed remorse before sentencing, while the victim's family described their ongoing trauma.

EPA found methyl bromide in a St. John vacation villa where a Delaware family fell ill, prompting an ongoing investigation. The toxic pesticide is banned for indoor use, and authorities are probing a possible fumigation at the resort. The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into the matter.

A Columbia Journalism School review found "institutional failure" at Rolling Stone led to a deeply flawed article about a University of Virginia gang rape. The magazine apologized for the damage caused. While UVA cannot sue for defamation as a public entity, members of the implicated Phi Kappa Psi fraternity may have grounds for a rare successful libel suit if they can prove the false story targeted their small, identifiable group and caused individual harm.

FBI agents shot and captured a serial robbery suspect in Georgia after he rammed their vehicles while attempting to flee a CVS pharmacy. Two agents were injured in the crash and the suspect sustained non-life-threatening gunshot wounds. The suspect is linked to 32 armed commercial robberies dating back to 2013.

An Alaska Airlines flight returned to Seattle after a ramp agent fell asleep in the cargo hold and was heard banging for help. The pressurized hold kept the man safe during the 14-minute flight, and he passed a drug test after being removed. The airline is investigating how the employee was left behind despite a pre-departure headcount.

A North Carolina judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks, accused of killing three Muslim students in Chapel Hill, is eligible for the death penalty. Hicks faces three counts of first-degree murder in the February shootings, which police said may have stemmed from a parking dispute but are also investigating as a possible hate crime.

Amnesty International reports Afghan women’s rights activists face rising attacks from the Taliban, warlords, and officials, with little government protection or accountability. The report highlights the mob killing of Farkhunda and the unprecedented female-led funeral protest as a sign of growing resistance. Activists warn that without stronger action, more women will be killed.

A New York court authorized serving divorce papers entirely via Facebook private message. Service of process law allows such digital alternatives when defendants evade traditional in-person delivery. Electronic service via private channels may be more effective and trackable than outdated methods like publication notices.

Televangelist Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" and Crystal Cathedral, died Thursday at 88. He built a media empire preaching an upbeat "possibility thinking" gospel before his ministry collapsed into bankruptcy and family infighting.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a massive fire on a Pemex oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico. The blaze, which started in the dehydration and pumping area, was extinguished after hours with no reported oil spill. About 300 workers were evacuated.

Kansas Governor Sam Brownback signed a first-of-its-kind US law banning the dilation and evacuation abortion procedure commonly used in the second trimester. Supporters hailed it as a groundbreaking measure to protect life, while opponents vowed legal challenges, calling it an extreme restriction that endangers women. The law permits the procedure only when necessary to save the mother's life or health.

Chinese state TV host Bi Fujian apologized after a video surfaced showing him cursing late Chairman Mao Zedong during a private dinner, sparking public controversy. CCTV said it would investigate the incident, which has divided online opinion in China. The clip was removed from domestic video sites but remained accessible on Weibo.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using a racial slur against Wisconsin’s Frank Kaminsky. Harrison said the remark was made in jest and he personally apologized to Kaminsky, who said he is “over it.”

“Arrested Development” will return for a 17-episode fifth season, executive producer Brian Grazer said on a podcast. Netflix declined to comment on the announcement. It is not yet known if the full cast will return.

The Large Hadron Collider has resumed operations after a two-year shutdown, circulating particle beams through its 17-mile ring. Scientists aim to use the high-energy collisions to investigate the origins of the universe, dark matter, and the incompleteness of the Standard Model. The machine will next be ramped up to record energy levels.

An Iranian military observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf, sparking concern that local Iranian forces may have acted without top commanders' approval. The unarmed aircraft made two close passes before the helicopter broke off, with U.S. officials suspecting the local commander was later reprimanded. The previously undisclosed incident risked escalation despite recent professional conduct by Iranian forces.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts for the Boston Marathon bombing, with 17 capital charges making him eligible for the death penalty. The trial now moves to a penalty phase where the jury will decide on execution after weighing aggravating and mitigating factors.

Four FabIndia employees arrested in Goa after a minister found a security camera pointed at a changing room. Police charged the staff with voyeurism and breach of privacy, while the store manager remains at large. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation.

Iran will partially lift its ban on women attending men's sports events within the next year, a deputy sports minister said. The change will apply to some indoor sports, though officials indicated restrictions will remain for events deemed uninteresting to families. The ban, in place since 1979, has drawn international pressure including from FIFA.

Ramalinga Raju, former chairman of Satyam Computers, and nine others were sentenced to seven years in prison for a $1.6 billion fraud. The case, India's largest corporate scandal, involved inflating profits with fictitious assets. Satyam was later acquired by Tech Mahindra after the government intervened.

An Alaska Airlines passenger with cancer was removed from a Hawaii flight after telling an employee she felt weak and lacking a doctor's note. The airline apologized, refunded her tickets, and paid for accommodations, but said the decision was made with her well-being in mind. The passenger said the delay caused her to miss chemotherapy.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan died of cancer Friday in Istanbul at age 66. The beloved love-song artist, whose career ignited after his 1991 album "I Made a Vow," had battled the disease since 1990. Prime Minister Davutoglu mourned the loss of a musician who marked a generation.

Israeli PM Netanyahu rejected the Iran nuclear framework as a "bad deal," advocating for increased pressure to secure better terms instead. He argued the deal leaves Iran's nuclear infrastructure intact and cannot be trusted, while U.S. officials and lawmakers continued to spar over its merits.

A domestic kidnapping sparked a shooting at the U.S. Census Bureau in Maryland, critically wounding a guard. The suspect fled, firing at multiple locations before crashing in Washington, D.C., where a shootout injured both the suspect and an officer. The kidnapping victim was found safe.

Imprisoned leaker Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating tweets by phone through a media firm as she lacks internet access. Manning, serving 35 years for leaking classified documents, said she wants the feed to be interactive. She is receiving hormone therapy at Fort Leavenworth after a legal name change.

Rapper Nelly was arrested in Tennessee after a traffic stop of his tour bus uncovered methamphetamine, marijuana, and drug paraphernalia. Troopers also found several handguns and 100 small Ziploc bags during the search. He was charged with felony drug possession and later released on bond.

A Delaware family fell critically ill at a U.S. Virgin Islands resort after their villa was contaminated with the restricted pesticide methyl bromide. The father is stable, the two sons remain critical, and the mother has been released. Federal authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the fumigation.

Online platforms have become the primary outlet for dissident voices in authoritarian Asian countries due to restricted access to traditional media. Governments like Singapore and Vietnam increasingly use legal and financial pressure to silence bloggers, while in Bangladesh, online critics of Islam face deadly attacks with near-total impunity.

Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving "The Vampire Diaries" after six seasons, upsetting fans who fear the show should end rather than continue without her. Producer Julie Plec supported Dobrev's decision, but many viewers expressed anger and sadness over the potential loss of closure for the "Delena" relationship.

ISIS fighters stormed Syria's Yarmouk Palestinian camp, triggering a government bombing campaign that has flattened buildings and trapped 18,000 residents without food or water. The camp, now controlled by an al Qaeda-linked group after ISIS withdrew, has become a grinding urban war zone where civilians face shelling and street combat. Despite the destruction, many residents refuse to leave their homes.

NASA scientists estimate 40 billion Earth-like planets exist in the Milky Way, making primitive life likely, but intelligent, communicative civilizations are extremely rare due to vast timescales and distances. Upcoming telescopes will search for biosignatures like oxygen in exoplanet atmospheres within decades.

A Massachusetts man faces murder charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge. Carlos Colina, 32, was already charged with assault and improper disposal of a body in connection with the death of Jonathan Camilien, 26. Additional remains were later discovered in a nearby apartment building.

Kanye West settled a civil lawsuit with a paparazzo he attacked at LAX in 2013, with the photographer's lawyer saying the settlement included an apology. The rapper had previously pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery and received probation.

Obama’s political legacy is so tied to an Iran deal that the U.S. appears the more desperate party, weakening its leverage. The framework leaves Iran as a nuclear threshold state with sanctions lifting early, while its record of concealment and regional aggression fuels distrust among anxious Arab allies.

A bystander's video of a South Carolina officer fatally shooting an unarmed black man has sparked outrage and murder charges, but highlights a critical data gap. A 1994 federal law requiring the collection of police use-of-force data has been largely ignored, leaving no comprehensive national record of such killings. This lack of mandatory reporting obscures the true scope of the problem and prevents analysis of racial bias or training failures.

Five Americans exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone have been released from a Nebraska hospital after three weeks of monitoring with no infections. One patient was briefly treated for a heart issue, while their infected colleague remains in fair condition at the NIH. The CDC expects the last of 17 monitored patients to be released by Thursday.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars leads the Billboard Hot 100 for a 13th week, becoming the longest-reigning No. 1 of the 2010s and one of only 10 singles in history to achieve the feat. The track simultaneously tops the Digital Songs, Radio Songs, and Streaming Songs charts for a record-extending ninth week. Meanwhile, newcomer Natalie La Rose enters the top 10 with her debut hit "Somebody."

April 8 was not only significant for "Lost" fans but also marked "Rex Manning Day" from the 1995 film "Empire Records." Other notable movie-inspired dates include April 14 ("Titanic"), April 25 ("Miss Congeniality"), October 3 ("Mean Girls"), and October 21, 2015 ("Back to the Future Part II").

“Grace of Monaco,” starring Nicole Kidman, will bypass U.S. theaters and premiere directly on Lifetime on May 25. The Weinstein Co. sold the critically-panned film to the network after its poor international performance and a public dispute with the director over the final cut.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance allowing "partnership certificates" for same-sex couples, granting limited rights like hospital visitation. While not legally binding marriages, activists call it a significant first step toward visibility and equality in socially conservative Japan.

California’s severe drought, now in its fourth year, threatens national food supplies as the state grows over a third of U.S. vegetables and two-thirds of fruits and nuts. While some grocery prices rose last year, a strong dollar and lower oil costs may offset further impacts, though reduced planting could still push prices higher. The drought is also forcing water-saving rules on restaurants and hotels, even as wine grape harvests thrive.

The University of Michigan reversed its cancellation of the film "American Sniper" after a student petition objecting to its portrayal of the Middle East drew backlash. Vice President E. Royster Harper said the initial decision was a mistake inconsistent with the school's free expression values. The screening will proceed alongside an alternative family-friendly film.

Amy Schumer's opening monologue and Channing Tatum's impromptu twerk for Jennifer Lopez were highlights of the 2015 MTV Movie Awards. Rebel Wilson's censored joke and Fall Out Boy's mashup with Fetty Wap also landed well. Misfires included a botched archery gag, Shailene Woodley's rambling speech, and a tired ball-grabbing bit from Zac Efron and Dave Franco.

A suspected piece of Japanese tsunami debris, a 20-to-30-foot boat fragment, was towed to Oregon carrying live yellowtail jack fish native to Japan. Biologists determined the invasive species threat was minimal. The fish will go to an aquarium while the wreckage is landfilled.

One year after Boko Haram kidnapped 276 schoolgirls in Chibok, Nigeria, over 200 remain missing. President-elect Muhammadu Buhari marked the anniversary with condolences, while the world renewed calls for their return. The mass abduction sparked global outrage but has yet to be resolved.

Easter's Triduum—Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday—ritualizes a universal human pattern of suffering, anxious transition, and transformative hope. The observance resists secular commercialization by embodying a spiritual progression from darkness into light.

Kenya froze 86 accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following the Garissa university massacre that killed 147 people. The government also launched airstrikes on militant camps in Somalia and offered a $215,000 bounty for the attack's alleged organizer. The moves come amid heavy criticism over the security response, as a rapid reaction team was reportedly delayed in Nairobi for hours.

Jia Jiang turned his fear of rejection into a viral project by making 100 bold requests to strangers, landing him a book deal and speaking career. His "Rejection Proof" philosophy argues that rejection is a numbers game and an opinion, not a personal verdict, and can be overcome by staying engaged and asking "why."

Attorney General Holder issued a memo to all Justice Department employees explicitly prohibiting the solicitation of prostitutes, even where legal, citing its link to human trafficking. The directive follows an inspector general report revealing DEA agents attended sex parties with prostitutes paid for by drug cartels. Violators face suspension or termination, regardless of whether they are on or off duty.

Police are investigating the fatal shooting of a Wayne Community College employee as a possible hate crime. The victim, a white gay man, was killed by a former work-study student with a shotgun. The suspect, who has facial tattoos and possible white supremacist ties, was arrested sleeping on a Florida beach.

Amnesty International reports a global rise in death sentences in 2014, driven by governments using executions as a misguided response to crime and terrorism. Despite a drop in recorded executions to 607, excluding China's secretive figures, countries like Pakistan and Jordan resumed capital punishment. The organization urges remaining executing states to join the 140 nations that have abolished the practice.

A Duke University student admitted to hanging a rope noose near a campus student union and is no longer on campus pending a conduct review. The university is investigating whether others were involved, and criminal inquiries are ongoing. The incident follows other recent racist acts on U.S. college campuses.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, best known for his role as senior partner Leland McKenzie on NBC's "L.A. Law," has died at 86. Dysart, who won an Emmy in 1992 for the role, died Sunday in Santa Monica after a long illness. His extensive career also included memorable film roles in "The Hospital," "Being There," and "The Thing."

Easter's date shifts annually based on the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox. The holiday's secular traditions, like the Easter bunny and colored eggs, likely originated with German immigrants in the 1700s. Pope Francis marked the day with an Easter Mass and an address lamenting global conflicts.

Comedian Chris Rock is highlighting racial profiling by documenting multiple recent traffic stops online. His posts come amid heightened national debate over racial disparities in policing. Some supporters praised his documentation, while one actor faced backlash for suggesting Rock change his vehicle to avoid stops.

Lynyrd Skynyrd's original drummer Robert Lewis Burns Jr. died in a single-car crash in Georgia at age 64. The musician was not wearing a seatbelt when his vehicle struck a mailbox and a tree. Burns left the band in 1975 and was not part of the 1977 plane crash that killed other members.

A viral photo of a cat on stairs has reignited the internet's love for optical illusions, sparking debate over whether the animal is ascending or descending. The image, spreading from Imgur to 9gag, has users analyzing the cat's gait and stair construction.

Framework agreed in Lausanne severely limits Iran’s capacity to build a nuclear bomb, cutting enriched uranium stockpiles and centrifuges while imposing permanent expanded inspections. Opponents’ claims that the deal aimed to eliminate Iran’s entire program or that it contains a sunset clause are factually incorrect. The agreement is a multilateral P5+1 deal, not a bilateral US pact, and mixing in unrelated issues would derail its core nonproliferation goal.

Rolling Stone retracted its article on an alleged gang rape at the University of Virginia after a review found reporting failures. The university faces ongoing investigations into its handling of sexual assault cases, having never expelled a student for it. Advocates fear the retraction could discourage survivors from coming forward.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed near a New York nightclub early Wednesday; he is in stable condition. Two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on obstruction charges after interfering at the crime scene. The suspect, who did not enter the club, was detained at the scene.

Twisted Sister announced their 2016 tour will be their last, marking their 40th anniversary with the "Forty and F*ck It" farewell tour. Mike Portnoy will join as drummer, replacing the late A.J. Pero, with two tribute shows planned in his honor.

John Travolta dismissed HBO's critical Scientology documentary "Going Clear," saying he hasn't seen it and doesn't care to. The actor called his 40-year experience with the church "brilliant" and credited it with helping him survive his son's death. He attributed the documentary to disgruntled former members and said he has no personal experience with the alleged negativity.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million opening weekend, with audiences deeply moved by its tribute to the late Paul Walker. The film retired Walker's character using body doubles and CGI, culminating in an emotional farewell montage that left many moviegoers in tears.

"Game of Thrones" season five will see major story arcs converge, including Tyrion and Daenerys, while moving beyond the published books. Executive producers promise bigger battles building toward a crescendo, with the Stark daughters and Cersei as key characters to watch. The season will also explore the common people's growing unrest with the nobles' endless wars.

Several individuals have survived weeks or months adrift at sea by relying on ingenuity, such as catching fish with laundry or drinking rainwater and turtle blood. Recent cases include a U.S. sailor rescued after 66 days off North Carolina and a fisherman who endured over a year in the Pacific before reaching the Marshall Islands. Rescuers emphasize such survival stories are exceptionally rare compared to the many that end in tragedy.

The "Star Wars" digital HD collection, releasing Friday, includes rare behind-the-scenes features. An exclusive video reveals sound designer Ben Burtt used animal noises to create the Geonosians' alien sounds.

Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts for the 2013 attack. Survivors and victims' families expressed relief and a step toward closure, though many said no verdict can fully heal their wounds. The conviction was hailed as a rejection of terrorism and a moment of accountability.

China's former security chief Zhou Yongkang was formally charged with bribery, abuse of power, and leaking state secrets. The 72-year-old ex-Politburo Standing Committee member is the highest-ranking official to face corruption charges. His trial marks a watershed moment in President Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption campaign.

Philadelphia police say a mother left her 21-year-old quadriplegic son with cerebral palsy in a park for over four days with only a blanket and Bible. The man was found suffering from dehydration, malnutrition, and infection, while his mother allegedly traveled to Maryland to visit her boyfriend. She faces multiple charges including aggravated assault, kidnapping, and neglect.

Walmart’s opposition to Arkansas’s religious freedom bill helped force the governor to demand changes, underscoring the retailer’s growing influence as a bellwether on gay rights and middle-class economic issues. The company’s stance reflects broader business community pressure against laws seen as discriminatory, with major firms and even NASCAR speaking out after Indiana passed similar legislation. Some Republicans, including Tim Pawlenty, say Walmart’s shift signals where the GOP must move to stay relevant.

A lapsed Catholic describes how Pope Francis's inclusive tone and emphasis on mercy over judgment rekindled her faith after feeling rejected by the church. A cardinal explains the Pope's approach mirrors Jesus by welcoming all without imposing, even while upholding traditional doctrine. The author resolves to return to church, moved by the message that the church does not reject sinners.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and Vili Fualaau, the former teacher and student whose sexual relationship sent her to prison, remain married ahead of their 10th anniversary. The couple discussed their marriage, her plans to teach again, and his struggles with alcoholism in an upcoming TV interview. She was 34 and he was 13 when the affair began in 1996.

Hillary Clinton's 2016 candidacy will unfairly serve as the sole barometer for US gender equality, burdening her with expectations no male candidate faces. A win risks complacency on women's issues, while a loss would perpetuate the myth that women cannot win top offices. However, partisanship and the economy, not gender, will ultimately determine the election's outcome.

Amnesty International reports governments are exploiting terrorism fears to justify executions, despite a global 22% drop in executions in 2014. However, death sentences surged 28% due to mass trials in countries like Egypt and Nigeria.

Japan's defense minister confirmed the Air Self-Defense Force has never encountered an extraterrestrial UFO, responding to a parliamentary query from wrestler-turned-lawmaker Antonio Inoki. The minister stated that while jets scramble for unidentified objects, all have been identified as birds or earthly aircraft.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce "Patriots' Day," a film about the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing told from the perspective of former Police Commissioner Ed Davis. The CBS Films project, drawing on "60 Minutes" material, is the second announced film about the attack.

Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb, both potential Democratic presidential candidates, displayed contrasting styles at an Iowa dinner, with O'Malley eagerly working the room while Webb remained more reserved. Both face long odds against Hillary Clinton, polling in the low single digits. Webb later appeared more at ease discussing veterans' issues at a separate event.

Nine British nationals, including four children, were arrested at the Turkey-Syria border suspected of attempting illegal entry into Syria. Turkish officials did not state the group's motive, but the region is a known route for Western

FedEx faces a 15-count federal indictment accusing it of conspiring with illegal online pharmacies to distribute controlled substances, despite the company arguing it is protected as a common carrier. The DOJ claims FedEx ignored years of warnings from regulators and its own couriers about suspicious shipments. The case tests whether a delivery company can be held criminally liable for the contents of packages it transports.

Kenyans are using the hashtag #147notjustanumber to share the stories of victims killed in the Garissa University College attack. The Al-Shabaab assault killed 147 people, mostly students, and is the nation's deadliest since the 1998 U.S. Embassy bombing. Authorities identified one slain gunman as the son of a government official who had reported him missing.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documents fathers using the country's generous 480-day parental leave, finding that only 12% of couples share it equally. His project captures the bonding and exhaustion of stay-at-home dads, aiming to present them as relatable role models.

President Obama affirmed his commitment to preserving Israel’s military edge over Iran while defending the nuclear framework deal. He argued the agreement offers a chance to remove the nuclear threat and increase oversight, even if Iran cannot be trusted. The deal faces criticism from Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and Republican lawmakers.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act has sparked national debate, but legal experts note that state-level religious liberty claims are rare and often involve minority faiths. Cases under similar laws have included a Native American's fight for eagle feathers, a Brazilian church's use of a hallucinogenic tea, and a Sikh IRS employee's ceremonial knife, with outcomes varying significantly.

Five Chinese feminist activists face up to five years in prison after police recommended charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order" for planned International Women's Day protests. The detentions have sparked international condemnation, with prosecutors expected to decide by Monday whether to pursue the case.

Tejano star Selena’s family is developing a “walking, talking, singing” digital embodiment of the late singer using Acrovirt technology. The project, “Selena the One,” aims to release new music, collaborate with current artists, and tour in 2018. An Indiegogo campaign seeking $500,000 launches April 16.

Former U.S. Representative Michele Bachmann likened President Obama to the Germanwings co-pilot who deliberately crashed his plane, calling him a "deranged pilot" flying the nation into the rocks with the Iran nuclear deal. Her comments drew widespread condemnation online as disrespectful and desperate.

Ryan Gosling’s directorial debut “Lost River” uses Detroit’s decay as its central character, with the film originating from his urgent footage of the condemned Brewster-Douglass Projects. The director says the movie captures both the city’s dangerous dereliction and its resilient, ongoing rebirth.

Yahya Rashid, 19, was charged with preparing and assisting acts of terrorism after being arrested at Luton Airport upon returning from Turkey. The charges cover a period from November 1 to March 31. He is due in Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe singer Vince Neil delivered a widely panned rendition of the U.S. national anthem before a Las Vegas Arena Football League game. His performance joins a list of infamous versions by Roseanne Barr and Michael Bolton, contrasting with Whitney Houston’s celebrated 1991 standard.

Nearly 2,000 WWI soldier inscriptions have been discovered in an ancient underground city near Naours, France. The graffiti, found after the site changed ownership in 2013, primarily names Australian and British troops who sheltered there, including many killed soon after in the Battle of the Somme.

The Palestinian Authority joined the ICC as its 123rd member, granting the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories since June 2014. The ICC has opened a preliminary examination that could lead to war crimes investigations against Israelis and Palestinians. Israel and the United States, non-members, opposed the move.

Anthony Ray Hinton was freed after nearly 30 years on Alabama’s death row after the state dropped murder charges against him. His 2014 retrial was ordered after firearms experts said the revolver used to convict him could not be matched to the crimes. Hinton, who always maintained his innocence, thanked God and his lawyers and said those responsible for his conviction would “answer to God.”

Tax refunds provide a psychological "happy ending" that makes most Americans overlook the system's deeper unfairness. The U.S. tax code increasingly favors wealth from capital over wages, but the average taxpayer focuses on the roughly $3,000 refund and free filing options. This short-term bliss obscures issues like marriage penalties and complexity that primarily benefit the rich.

Jordan Spieth maintained a commanding four-shot lead at the Masters despite a late double bogey, as rivals including Justin Rose and Phil Mickelson failed to significantly close the gap on Moving Day.

Liana Barrientos pleaded not guilty to charges she falsified a 2010 marriage license application, part of an alleged immigration scam involving 10 marriages. Prosecutors say she was married to eight men at once, with some husbands filing for residency after the weddings. She was also arrested Friday for allegedly sneaking into the subway.

Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, faced backlash and boycott calls after its owners said they would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding, citing their religious beliefs under the state’s Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The controversy drew both harsh criticism and a wave of support, with an online fundraiser collecting over $842,000 for the family-run business.

Mindy Kaling’s brother Vijay Chokalingam revealed he posed as black on medical school applications to expose what he calls unfair affirmative action advantages. He received only one admission offer, from a lower-ranked school, and says he experienced racial profiling while pretending to be black. The article argues his case actually undermines his claim and highlights the need for diversity programs in medicine and media.

Antarctica recorded a temperature of 63.5°F (15.5°C) on March 24, potentially its highest ever. The World Meteorological Organization is assembling a committee to verify the reading. Researchers monitor such extremes for evidence of global warming.

The U.S. is no longer setting a timeline for an Iraqi-led offensive to retake Mosul from ISIS, with officials saying it could happen soon or much later. While airstrikes have begun softening ISIS positions, a full ground assault is not imminent due to the city's size and complexity.

Irish bookmaker Paddy Power deleted a tweet joking that Newcastle suffered more “Kop beatings” than an unarmed African-American male, drawing widespread condemnation. The company said no offense was intended, but the removal failed to quell outrage over the reference to U.S. police killings.

Philadelphia police added attempted murder to the charges against Nyia Parler, who allegedly left her quadriplegic son in a park for days. Parler remains in Maryland receiving unspecified treatment and cannot be extradited until it is completed. The 21-year-old son, who has cerebral palsy, was found covered in leaves with a Bible and wheelchair nearby.

South Korean prosecutors indicted Kim Ki-Jong for attempted murder and assaulting a foreign envoy over last month's knife attack on U.S. Ambassador Mark Lippert. The suspect, who opposed joint U.S.-South Korea military drills, faces trial within 14 days. Lippert suffered deep facial wounds requiring 80 stitches but avoided permanent nerve damage.

Jill Duggar Dillard of "19 Kids and Counting" gave birth to her first child, a son named Israel David. The baby arrived more than a week past his due date. Dillard is the first of the Duggar daughters to become a mother.

“Furious 7” is racing toward a $135 million-plus domestic opening, the largest since 2013. The Paul Walker tribute earned a record $60 million internationally in two days, putting its global debut on track to near $300 million. It will easily become the top April opening and the biggest launch of 2015.

A Secret Service supervisor was placed on leave after being accused of sexually assaulting a female employee. The alleged assault occurred after a party celebrating his new assignment. The incident adds to a series of recent scandals plaguing the agency.

Hillary Clinton announces her 2016 presidential bid, bringing extensive experience but facing challenges including authenticity doubts, base enthusiasm, and potential liabilities from her husband. Her campaign plans smaller events to avoid the perception of inevitability that hurt past candidates.

The Justice Department will soon negotiate a court-enforced overhaul of Ferguson's police and courts, following a probe that found systemic racial discrimination and profit-driven policing. Recent elections have added two Black council members and the police chief has resigned, but lasting reform hinges on upcoming DOJ talks and sustained community pressure.

Etihad Airways lost a passenger's pet cat at New York's JFK Airport after its carrier was crushed during a flight from Abu Dhabi. The airline is investigating and has hired specialists to search for the missing animal. The owner criticized the carrier's handling, saying the cat was treated like cargo.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued by a container ship after drifting at sea for 66 days when his sailboat capsized off the South Carolina coast. He survived by collecting rainwater and netting fish attracted to his laundry, and was found in surprisingly good condition. The Coast Guard said it has no reason to doubt his account.
